record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.context_brief: DBT under stress and cyclic protocols
record.original_question: Does the ductile-to-brittle transition observed mainly under constant shear-rate, simple-plane-shear forcing also occur under constant external stress or cyclic shear, and what quantitative measure of brittleness can compare different geometries, protocols, materials, and simulations?

evidence.quote: Moreover, it is important to understand whether or not the DBT also occurs under a constant external stress and/or in cyclic shear protocol. In order to compare the DBT in different geometries and under various testing protocols, both in experiments and in numerical computations, it is essential to introduce a quantitative measure of brittleness.
Defining and investigating similar observables in soft glassy systems should help characterize the DBT and identify universal features, if any , common to soft and hard materials.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft amorphous material (such as a colloidal glass, emulsion, foam, gel, or simulated Lennard–Jones glass) modeled as a disordered assembly of particles that, in the solid state, exhibits a yielding transition under mechanical loading. Under constant shear-rate simple-plane-shear forcing, such materials are known to display a ductile-to-brittle transition (DBT): for sufficiently well-annealed initial states, yielding occurs abruptly via a macroscopic stress drop accompanied by the formation of a sharp shear band, while for poorly annealed states yielding is a smooth crossover with diffuse plasticity.

Address the following two coupled questions:

(a) Does an analogous DBT occur for the same class of materials when the loading protocol is replaced by (i) a constant external shear stress (creep-type forcing) and/or (ii) cyclic (oscillatory) shear at fixed strain amplitude and frequency? Formulate precise criteria (in terms of macroscopic stress–strain response, strain-field localization, energy release, or microstructural precursors) that detect the existence of such a transition in these protocols and either establish or rule out its occurrence.

(b) Construct a single quantitative scalar measure of "brittleness" B, defined intrinsically from observables of the yielding response (e.g., normalized stress overshoot, magnitude and rate of stress drop, energy released at failure, width of shear bands, distribution of avalanche sizes, or features of the loss modulus in oscillatory tests) such that B can be unambiguously evaluated across:
  – different loading geometries (simple shear, pure shear, extension, indentation, etc.),
  – different protocols (constant strain rate, constant stress, oscillatory shear),
  – different materials (soft glasses, metallic glasses, polymer glasses, granular packings), and
  – both experimental and numerical (molecular-dynamics, mesoscale elasto-plastic) realizations,
and such that B varies monotonically and reproducibly with the degree of annealing or other control parameter driving the DBT. Prove or demonstrate that the proposed B is protocol- and geometry-independent in this sense.
artifact.category_tag: Yielding and ductile-to-brittle transition in amorphous solids
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature (2024–2026) continues to describe the existence of the ductile-to-brittle transition under non-shear-rate protocols (constant stress, cyclic shear) and a universal protocol-independent measure of brittleness as outstanding open problems. Partial results exist (e.g., brittility factor, stress-overshoot criteria, activity-induced annealing studies, finite-disorder critical-point analyses), but no consensus quantitative measure unifying geometries, protocols and materials has been established.

status_evidence.title: Activity-induced annealing leads to a ductile-to-brittle transition in amorphous solids
status_evidence.snippet: Recent (2024) study of DBT induced by annealing in amorphous solids.
status_evidence.claim: Active research area; transition mechanisms still being elucidated.

status_evidence.title: Brittle and ductile yielding in soft materials
status_evidence.snippet: Introduces brittility factor based on rheological signatures (stress overshoot, loss modulus peak).
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress toward a brittleness measure, but not yet universal across all protocols/geometries.

status_evidence.snippet: 2026 study identifying a finite-disorder critical point separating brittle and ductile yielding.
status_evidence.claim: Topic remains under active investigation in 2026.
